1. Atrium (b): regular and harmonious was the arrangement of the rooms on the N side of the atrium with the tablinum in a central position. The pillars in opus vittata, probably redone, were covered only with rough plaster and awaited the final painting.
2. Atrium (b): the impluvium had a marble edge with a simple rather rigid reverse kyma molding.  '79 N52180

3. Cubicle (d): not painted in the last period of Pompeii's life, the small room still retained the frescoed surfaces at the time of the excavation on which the attributes of Artemis (So, 114) "The crouching deer, the quiver and a golden crown" and "Three dancing erotes" (So, 349) could be distinguished, among other decorative elements.

4. Cubicle (e): the decoration of this room was complete and was rather simple with the red plinth divided into a central compartment with a bush with long lanceolate leaves and two panels crossed by edges of triangle carpet. The white middle area was a bipartite structure with the narrow central compartment crossed by a twisted candelabrum between the panels. The upper white area divided into squares outlined in red, is followed by the lunette with stucco frames along the chord and along the arch of the lowered arch that constituted the false ceiling of the cubicle.
5. Cubicle (e): detail of the stucco frames of the lunette preserved on the N wall, with circumscribed acanthus leaves.

6. Cubicle (e): the squares of the side panels consisted of carpet edges with symmetrical buds that were particularly evident on the white background as they were fields in red and preserved in faint traces on the wall E in the thickness of which the exhaust pipe of the upper floor passed, visible in the hole at the N end.

7. Cubicle (f): on the N wall the scheme of the decoration, common to the other walls, is still legible, with only the details of the red plinth divided into a central compartment with a four-petal rosette and the side panels with flowering iridaceous plants. In the middle white area, with a similar bipartite structure, but we do not know on which of the walls these are now completely washed out or for the most part devoid of plaster, there were, among others, vignettes of "a cupid with a bunch of grapes in the raised right" (So, 285) and of "a crowned and naked female figure, except for a veil that falls from her arms behind her shoulders,  he carries in his right hand a face and in his left a basket of flowers" (So, 795).

8. Tablinum (g): the greater refinement put into the decoration of this room, in a central position with respect to the atrium and the entrance, can still be grasped despite the ravages of time and the gaps produced by the removal of the central painting with the portraits of the owners of the house and the group, inserted between the architecture of the upper area, of Cupid and Psyche. The red plinth, which in the central compartment exhibited a plant, in the side panels above the edge of the square carpet showed garlands on which peacocks were resting. In the middle area, the white central compartment separated the yellow side panels in one of which the fresco with "Nike resting on a shelf and carrying a trophy on his left shoulder" (So, 438), reproduced by La Volpe in 1868, was seen but already "almost vanished" (cf. ADS 530; see Draftsmen, p. 744, fig. 213).

9. Tablinum (g): the painting with the portrait of Terentius Neo with his wife (65 x 58) is now in the Museum of Naples (inv. 9058) and is among the most famous pieces in the collection of frescoes for the expressive immediacy of the faces realistically portrayed by a specialized painter and not by a generic pictor parietarius who,  drawing on the available repertoire, he would have re-proposed regular faces, with well-proportioned features to be traced back to the category of types and not to that of portraits. The accentuated triangular face, the large eyes with an intense expression, the ears away from the head, the short beard of the man, the hairstyle of the woman absolutely realistic and datable to the middle of the first century AD, make this painting a real portrait, revealing the painter's commitment not to deviate from the real appearance of the characters depicted to whom he tried to give an intellectual attitude. The mannered pose of the man in a toga and with his face resting on the kneecap held tightly in his hand, and of the woman with the stylus brought to her lips and the diptych open to the viewer, to flaunt her skill in writing (in a society in which knowing how to read and write was not for everyone), was not, however, enough to ennoble her features and to convince the viewer of the painting,  that the couple was of high social status. The popular origin and the embarrassment of the couple posing in their best clothes, awkwardly still in front of the painter's brush, have been happily rendered by him, and make this one of the most singular paintings among those returned from the Vesuvian cities.

10. Tablinum (g): the group with Cupid and Psyche (So, 394), detached from the centre of the upper area of the N wall with the painted window within which it was inserted and beyond which a rafters can be seen, is now in Naples at the National Museum (inv. 9195). 11. Tablinum (g): the walls E and W were both in opus craticium and ended near the jamb in opus listatum which is the only one to preserve traces of the pictorial decoration in the remains of the red plinth.

12. Triclinium (h): originally intended as a tablinum, this room changed its function in the last period of the house's life, but retained the primitive decoration in particular on the N wall, which did not undergo changes. The black plinth was divided into panels and compartments like the yellow middle area in which the central panel exhibits a taut carpet bordered by a thin garland with the resulting spaces covered in purple. The same color constitutes the bottom of the compartments crossed by white candelabras, which separate the center from the side panels with carpet borders and medallions. The medallion E with the depiction of a "bust of a beardless young man, in profile with red chlamys attached to the left humerus holding a staff in his right" (So, 635) was detached, the one O is barely preserved in traces. In the upper white area, separated from the one below by a purple band, you could see "squares, aedicules and landscapes".

13. Triclinium (h): in the centre of the taut carpet in the middle area was the vignette of a cupid (So, 256) advancing to the right with the chlamys descending from his left arm and the quiver in his hands.

14. Triclinium (h): in panel O of the N wall the traces of the medallion with a female bust interpreted as Atalanta by the first descriptors (GdS 1868, c. 62) are still legible to compare it to the male bust of the same wall, inter489

15. Triclinium (h): there is no information about the presence on wall E, of any subjects figured in the yellow side panels of the middle area divided by the presence of the central purple compartment.

16. Triclinium (h): the decoration of the room, and therefore of the wall O, had already been carried out when, having purchased the ius luminum on the adjoining courtyard of the dyeing house 11, the master of the house was able to open this large window which interrupted the frescoes executed, which were still quite legible in the details of the central panels with a yellow stretched carpet,  purple side panels and white upper area with schematic architecture. Part of the stucco frame with a lesbian kyma motif that crowned the frescoed area also remains.

17. Triclinium (h): the S wall that separates the triclinium from the corridor (i), was made of opus craticium, better legible on the opposite face and leaning against the O wall of which he interrupted the decoration. Traces of the plaster painted yellow are preserved to match the dominant colour in the primitive decoration of the room.

18. Corridor (i): the view from the S clearly reveals the masonry technique used to create this partition created to define and separate the entrance to the kitchen from the original tablinum transformed into a triclinium. The wall was covered with painted plaster that retains its blazing yellow color.

19. Corridor (i): the S wall of the corridor was originally the left wall of the tablinum, of which it retains the same decorative scheme with the carpet stretched in the central panel, separated from the side panels by compartments with a purple background with candelabra and medallions in the yellow side panels. The decorative motifs of the upper white area are illegible, while the stucco frame is discreetly preserved.

20. Corridor (i): in the E section of the S wall there was a painted medallion (diameter 28 cm) with a bust of Paris with pedum and the cupid behind his shoulder, caressing his chin (So, 557), known from the drawing by N. La Volpe ADS 531 (see Disegnatori, p. 746, fig. 215).

21. Corridor (i): as a pendant on the opposite section of the same wall, there was the medallion (diameter 28 cm) with the bust of Helen (So, 556) "veiled, adorned with a golden diadem and turned to the left", also documented by the same drawings by La Volpe mentioned in fig. previous.
22. Corridor (i): the medallions of figs. 20-21, in the drawing by N. La Volpe.

23. The corridor (m) was deprived of the partition that separated this house from the nearby pistrinum 3, becoming the connecting route between the two complexes. In the cocciopesto cladding, the holes corresponding to the housings of shelves or other, in use in the previous destination, were occluded with cocciopesto of different workmanship. 79 N52182

1. Workshop (1): on the N wall there is a long masonry staircase made of opus incerta with a round support arch and a brick pillar as a support structure. Of the pictorial decoration, which must not have been completely anonymous, very few traces remain just below the staircase.

2. Workshop (1): the intrados of the arch under the stairs preserves few remains of the decoration that showed a fake opus quadratum outlined in red on a white background, with a dotted rosette in each of the panels. 79 N52215

1. On the pillar to the left of the entrance hall was painted the figure of an offector with clothes hanging from a pole that was documented by Abbate in a drawing of 1844 (ADS 1222; see Disegnatori, p. 305, fig. 104) therefore executed when only the façade of the block had been brought to light. The fall of the plaster highlighted the brick structure of the jambs of the large entrance hall, probably built after the earthquake of 62 AD.

2. Entrance hall (a); The characteristics of the limestone threshold with the groove outwards to house the door with movable axes, and on the left the recess for the hinge of the leaf of a door stopped with an up-and-down latch, are typical of a workshop and not of a stately home that would have had a normal double-leaf door.

3. Entrance hall (a); the S walls retain faded traces of the plaster painted in the IV style in which the middle area can still be distinguished, above the black plinth, with a central yellow panel separated from the side panels whose colour is not intuitive, by compartments bordered in red.

4. The view from S-0 of the peristyle (b) allows us to still grasp its original appearance with the Ionic columns with fluted shafts covered with white plaster, which supported the roof of the porticoes before the transformation into a dyeing plant.

5. Peristyle (b); the W portico had already been abolished to create the tablinum (n) from the large entrance, flanked by the cubicles (o) on the left with which it also had direct communication, and (p) on the right that took light from the rectangular windows placed within the alignment of the colonnades, so as to better take the light from the valley. In the foreground some of the masonry furnaces and the lava stone basin.

6. Peristyle (b); next to the oecus (1) is the staircase (K) to the upper floor, made of masonry and leaning against a wall in opus incerta, the head of which was reinforced with brick fills probably after the earthquake, a period to which the reconstruction of the brick column must also be traced, whose capital, like that of the adjoining column in the SW corner,  it was replaced by a simple Tuscan capital.

7. Peristyle (b); the NE corner, in which the cubicle opens (f), preserves evident traces of the original masonry structures in opus a frame with the use of blocks of limestone from the Sarno and uncertain work with stones of various sizes, mostly lava, dating back to the III-II century BC. The renovation of the complex, on the other hand, dates back to the chiseling of the grooves of the column in the foreground.  79 N52208

9. Peristyle (b); the engraving visible in the block of the stylobate of the N-E corner, without the column, allows us to verify that the intersection of the two graffiti axes indicated the point at which the center of the base of the column should fall, which was moved towards the inside of the porticoes, the stylobate being part of the molding towards the channel.  79 N52218

8. Peristyle (b), N portico; The care taken by the builders of the peristyle, detectable in the presence of guide lines engraved in the blocks of the stylobate to indicate the point of support of the columns, indicates that the primitive building belonged to a client of high social position or at least of considerable economic level.   79 N52240

10a-b. Peristyle (b); the capitals (140-120 BC), like the columns, were entirely covered with white plaster which gave the tuff, preciously sculpted, the appearance of the most expensive marble.  79 N52204 - N52203

10a-b. Peristyle (b); the capitals (140-120 BC), like the columns, were entirely covered with white plaster which gave the tuff, preciously sculpted, the appearance of the most expensive marble.  79 N52204 - N52203

11. Peristyle (b); Next to the channel deeply hollowed out in tuff blocks is the mouth of the cistern below the peristyle, into which rainwater flowed through the conspicuous hole in the channel itself.  79 N52236
13. Peristyle (b); in the N intercolumnium of the E portico there is a rectangular lava basin.  79 N52188

12. Peristyle (b); in the N portico there was the mouth of a terracotta cistern with the frames characterized by a decoration obtained with the impression, freehand, of very simple tools, perhaps only a reed used vertically for the undulations and horizontally for the circles, attributable to the beginning of the first century BC.

14. Peristyle (b); in the N portico two ovens were built in opus incerta with lava vents. On them rested the containers for hot dyeing the fabrics; To facilitate the work of the offectores who had to reach the top of the tubs, a ladder had also been built between the two high hillocks.

15. Peristyle (b); in portico E there were seven ovens of different heights. In the background, beyond the entrance hall, the entrance to the cubicle (e) is recognized, made with the division into two rooms, by means of the partition in opus incerta, of an original large cubicle.
16. Peristyle (b); The ovens, close to each other, also lean against the entrance wall to the room (I) which had a vaulted roof of which the sturdy impost kidneys remain.  79 N52211

17. Cubicle (f). The cubicle function of this small room is attested by the recess for the bed in the N wall at the height of the plinth and beyond the attachment of the middle area underlined by a green horizontal stripe. 79 N52202
18. The cubicle (f) was decorated in the III style still recognizable in the black plinth sprinkled with yellow and red, and in the middle area divided into yellow and black panels.
19. Cubicle (f); on the S wall there are traces of the yellow side panel and the black central panel.

20. Cabinet (g); in a recess in the N wall a wardrobe was placed with several wooden shelves fixed in the walls on which were the glass containers with the colors necessary for the dyeing activity, partly found at the time of the excavation.

21. The oecus (1) divided into antechamber and hall, preserved in the latter conspicuous elements of the decoration of the initial II style with a black and green podium on which rested columns behind which were arranged orthostats and ashlars bordered at the top by cornices, ovoli and friezes, of such a chromatic ensemble that Mau (Mau W, p.- 272) emphasized their proximity to the colors of the first style,  if it hadn't been for the presence of violet instead of cinnabar. On the wall $S now there are only traces of the completely washed plaster.

22. Cubicle (m); the decoration of the second style, of which traces are preserved on the O wall, dates back to a period prior® to the subdivision of this room from the nearby cubicle (0) as the partition raised for the purpose partially covers it. This also explains the anomalous presence, in the decorative scheme described by Mau (Mau W, p. 272), of a single column with a smooth shaft (distinguishable just in correspondence with the large restored gap and the double row of iron clamps), from which, silhouetted against the violet of the background of the upper area above the rafters seen in foreshortening,  hung a garland of ivy. From what remains you can recognize the plinth interrupted by the recess for the bed then walled up and covered with rough plaster, the middle area with purple and yellow orthostats surmounted by rows of green and yellow rectangular ashlars and purple squares.

23. Tablinus (n); the fall from the O wall of the most superficial layers of the plaster, only partially preserved in the S corner, show in the N corner the traces left by the trowel on the fresh plaster at the time of application.

24. VII 2, 12. Workshop, room (1): the workshop located to the N of the vestibule was part of the primitive nucleus of the house, in which "nothing else can be seen except the staircase of the mezzanine and the niche of the Penates" (Fiorelli D, p. 185) on the O wall which shows, together with the pillars that delimit the entrance, a sample of masonry techniques, the result of restoration work that became necessary after the earthquake of 62 AD.

25. VII 2, 12. Workshop, room (1): in the N-E corner of the room there is the masonry ladder to the mezzanine reachable through another wooden ramp whose practicability must have been caused by the bulky drain pipe made up of terracotta cylinders. 79 N52234

1. Bottegaal 13. The oldest structure in opus a frame is evident, preserved in the back wall, compared to the side walls in opus vittata mixed with brick recurrences, carried out as part of the restoration work following the earthquake of 62 AD. The walled door gave access to the atrium (c) of the house at number 14.

2. Vestibule (b); the walls of the entrance room were redone in opus incerta with recurrences of bricks placed at the base and at the top of the walls, reinforced towards the outside by the pillars in opus vittata. The total lack of traces of plaster from them suggests that the redecoration of this part of the house had not yet taken place.

3. Atrium (c); the N wall in particular still retains the large quadrangular blocks of tuff that denote its belonging to the third century BC; particularly accurate in the E wall are the insertions of the bricks in the previous masonry, especially near the jambs.
4. Atrium (c); the impluvium in tuff slabs, belonging to type A for the type of molding of the edge, had been chiselled along the N and E sides to house marble cladding slabs.   79 N61542

5. Atrium (c); the N wall, in which the door of the triclinium (d) opens, presents a frame work of execution particularly accurate in the choice of well-squared and large blocks for the construction of the stone framework, completed with uncertain work mainly of tuff.
6. Atrium (c); the S wall was raised using grooved fragments of Sarno limestone, and the so-called lava cruma for filling. Traces of the plaster coating remain at the height of the plinth.  79 N61562

7. Triclinium (d), N wall with the two splayed windows, of different heights open onto the Vicolo del Panettiere. The type of pictorial decoration, as far as can still be seen, with a high pinkish plinth and the upper area apparently devoid of decorative elements, would confirm the hypothesis of a public use of the room, serving the taberna at no. 15 with which it was intercommunicating. 79 N61550

8. Tablinum (e), remains of a mosaic floor: the threshold was characterized by the motif of swastika meanders alternating with a square containing a central rectangle; the field of white tesserae arranged in an oblique warp was dotted with irregularly scattered polychrome tesserae, the edge was made up of a band of black tesserae between two rows of white tesserae arranged in a straight warp, the marginal flounce resumed, as usual, the oblique course.

9. Tablinum (e), wall N: currently (1995) there is no longer any trace of the painted plaster present on this wall made at the beginning of the first century BC, as indicated by the use of the almost reticulated work. At the time of the excavation (1867) the paintings of not large dimensions (0.55 x 0.55) were also preserved. On the left was a Nereid on a sea ox, accompanied by two erotes, and on the right a Satyr discovering a Maenad. The plinth was purple, divided into panels with triangle carpet edges, while the upper area was already illegible. '79 N61546

10. Tablinum (e), S wall: the structure of the wall is not recognizable, which in the middle area with a yellow background exhibited two paintings: on the left a Judgement of Paris, and on the right a Nereid on a sea horse, accompanied by a dolphin.

11. Tablinum (e), S wall: the painting executed in a current manner and with some awkwardness in proportioning the figures and architectural details to each other, depicts the Judgement of Paris, with the young shepherd, in oriental clothes, exhorted by Hermes to turn towards the group of the three goddesses. These, as usual well characterized by clothing, pose and attributes, and in the same scheme, albeit inverted, of the picture of the

12. Tablinum (e); wall O with the window towards the viridarium (1). Traces of the purple plinth were preserved with panels containing a singular motif of a carpet border with triangles entirely fielded, and separated by compartments with plants. In the yellow middle area, above the window, there was another painting with a seascape with boats, buildings and men including a fisherman.

13. Section O of the corridor (f) leads to room (i), which is also illuminated through the quadrangular window, and to the kitchen (h) located lower than the other domestic rooms. Of the staircase to the upper floor, only the masonry podium leaning against the S wall remains, visible on the left.

14. Room (k): on the S wall there are evident recesses for housing the support beams of the floor of a floor above plastered in a way that is probably different from the lower one which retains only a discolored plaster.

15. Viridarium(1); the watercolour reproduction of the N-W corner of this room, made in 1881, showed the decoration almost complete, as today it can only be reconstructed in shreds due to the almost total fall of the plaster especially from the W wall. The continuity between the two walls was given by the motif of leaves, bunches, pelte and oscilla hanging from an imaginary architrave that defined the "windows" open onto a garden with fountains and statues on the two walls. While

16. Viridarium (l), N wall, section W with the masonry altar, now completely disappeared, towards which the snake crawls, partly hidden by the oleander bushes. Above, from the left, we can recognize: Jupiter with the chlamys, the Lares on either side of the cylindrical altar and Athena with helmet, shield and spear.

17. Viridarium (1), N wall; detail of the figure of Jupiter with the sceptre in his right hand, the red chlamys resting on his left shoulder; In his left hand, stretched out towards the center, Laquila.

18. Viridarium (1), N wall; on the sides of a cylindrical altar on which the fire is lit, two Lares drop the gush of the liquid contained in the horns, into the golden situle that they hold in their hands.

19. Lararium (1), N wall; detail of the figure of Athena dressed as the Promachos with a crested helmet, shield and spear brandished in her right hand, with a small owl at her feet; It seems to re-propose the figure of the goddess in the painting of the Tablinum (E).

20. Viridarium (1); on the N wall there is a window towards the corridor (f) and on the left jamb there are the remains of a male figure with a short white chlamys who walks towards the scene of the sacrifice holding "indefinable" objects in his hands already at the time of the excavation; although larger than those of the other figures, it could be the representation of a bidder.

21. Viridarium(1); the S wall of the room, just 2.90 m wide, is interrupted in the center by a large quadrangular window that illuminated the cubicle (m) and by an arched niche; white plaster does not retain traces of other colors or figurative elements.
22. Viridarium (1); in the extreme W section, the S wall bends into a niche perhaps used as a wardrobe before the garden area was arranged.   79 N61539
23. Viridarium (1), W wall; The remains of the garden painting interrupted in the center by the insertion of a stroke of white plaster and a square niche are barely distinguishable.
24. Viridarium (1), wall O: detail of the $ corner with bunches of grapes hanging from the architrave painted in yellow against the blue background of the sky.

25. Cubicle (m); the N wall, interrupted by the large window open onto the viridarium (1), is also the best preserved of the whole room. On the white background, the plinth outlined by a green frame, the panel of the middle area bordered by taut garlands and with a central medallion, the frame of the window made up of red and black bands can be recognized. '79 N61567

26. Cubicle (m), wall N: the extreme simplicity of the decoration is associated with an equally particular accuracy in the execution of the details. The stretched garland framing the panel is traced with the help of guidelines engraved on a polished area to allow the recarbonation of the lime, the central medallion is also drawn with the help of the compass.
27. Cubicle (m), N wall; only this female head remains, painted in a medallion (diameter 17 cm) of the "several round paintings representing female heads" seen at the time of the excavation.

28. Cubicle (m), S wall, in which the fall of the plaster has highlighted the existence of a closed door, once a passage to the room (p) of the nearby house at number 11. In the central panel, instead of the medallion, there was a painting (33 x 177) completely illegible. 79 N61568
29. Cubicle (m), W wall; The roof of the room was a barrel vault, with the lunettes bordered by molded stucco frames, set above the upper white area which showed, in this section, red squares.

30. The workshop at number 15, located at the corner of the insula, identifiable as taberna due to the presence of the masonry counter that limited the large entrance, was in direct communication with the rooms (a), and therefore (d), of the house. Its walls had been extensively restored with discontinuous insertions of bricks, while the external pillars were completely redone.

31. Bottega at number 15.Il counter that leaned against the wall in opus incerta, tending to be almost reticulated, with the ladder for the display of food, ended in the arm folded towards the inside of the room, with the housing for the boiler for cooked dishes. The plaster on the S wall is heavily worn and appears as rough. 79 N61561

1. The façade of the house preserves the frame structures with the jambs in limestone blocks completed at the top by cubic capitals of tuff that confirm its dating at least to the second century BC. The modern plaque with the indication of the name of the alleged owner follows the traditional name contested by Della Corte as it derives from an incorrect reading of graffiti on the plaster of this façade.
2. Under the lava blocks of the sidewalk you can see the hole for the drainage of waste water from the house through a channel passing under the threshold.

3. The vestibule (a), separated from the atrium by a door that closed on the high lava threshold with hinge housings, allowed access to the ostianii cell (1), whose lava threshold is also visible on the right and from this to the stable (b) whose function was recognized by the arrangement on the walls of the holes for the planks of the manger and for the rustic appearance of the room. The floor was made of cocciopesto with flakes of limestone and blue-gray breccia. II initial style.

4. Atrium (c); The room of almost square proportions had the side walls interrupted only at the back wall by the doors of the rooms (F), (G) and at the back it opened immediately towards the peristyle (H) since the tablinum was not in the canonical position. On the walls, partly restored with insertions of brickwork, only the layer of rough plaster had been laid and the final decoration had yet to be carried out.
5. Atrium (c); The jambs of the door towards the portico (E) had been reinforced with the addition of brick pillars inserted in the previous masonry only in the lower part.

6. Atrium (c); The floor has the unusual combination of limestone and mosaic. The first technique was used for the marginal band in which sparse yellow, black, red and green scales are inserted, and for the field in which the polychrome scales are denser and are also accompanied by black tiles. The border was made in mosaic with nine rows of black tesserae between two and three rows of white tesserae. II initial style. The marble-clad impluvium, to be attributed to a modernization of the house, was connected to a cistern below, whose primitive mouth is indicated by the position of the manhole cover that replaced it but with smaller dimensions as there was no longer the need to draw water. The lead fistula visible at the bottom ended near the impluvium in the base of a statuette of Faun. This was accompanied by a dog from whose mouth the gush came out and filled a basin from which it fell into the impluvium. The passage to the portico (e) of the peristyle was limited by a limestone threshold in which the dimensions of the two leaves of the door can be reconstructed from the arrangement of the recesses for the hinges and bolts.

7. Atrium (c); detail of the N-W corner in which the continuity of installation between the beaten and mosaic parts can be seen, a detail that excludes the hypothesis of the subsequent insertion of the tessellated band.

8. Cubicle (d); the room, originally painted in the first style, was redecorated at the beginning of the first century BC and on that occasion the cocciopesto floor was also redone in which, as a characteristic motif of the second style, there are rows of crosses. The bedside rug and the threshold towards the wardrobe are made up of a motif of swastika meanders alternating with concentric squares; the threshold towards the atrium was made of fragments of African marble, now completely disappeared, while the narrow slabs of lava placed in correspondence with the jambs remain.

9. Cubicle (d); detail of the N-W corner of the cocciopesto floor in which the carpet of staggered rows of white crosses with a black center is bordered by a single row of black tesserae placed side by side.

10. Cubicle (d): the NW corner retained part of the decoration in the first style because it was transformed into a wardrobe with the construction of the partition in opus incerta, before the repainting in the second style of all the parts that would have been visible. The hero's mother holds a greaves and the Centaur holds a shield, embossed with a dolphin and a spear.
